elements.element: Customer has no non-compete or field-of-use restriction.
elements.evidence: The prohibitory second § 12.4 ("During the term and for twenty-four months thereafter, Customer shall not develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor...") is replaced with an affirmative permission: "12.4 Customer may develop, market, sell, or acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory." No compete, field-of-use, or territory restriction binding Customer remains, and § 12.3 still records that Customer has made no non-compete commitment. Deterministic check "no open-ended compete restriction on Customer remains" is ok.

elements.element: The restriction covers only a named competing product.
elements.evidence: Vacuously satisfied: after the edit there is no restriction on Customer at all (§ 12.4 is now a permission), so the condition on which this element operates does not apply. The narrowed named-product fallback is only offered in the margin comment, not in operative text.

elements.element: The restriction applies during the term only.
elements.evidence: Vacuously satisfied: no restriction survives; the 24-month post-term tail was removed with the prohibition. No temporal restriction on Customer remains anywhere in §§ 12.3–12.4.

elements.element: The restriction lasts no longer than 12 months.
elements.evidence: Vacuously satisfied: the 24-month duration was deleted and no replacement duration or restriction exists, so no period can exceed 12 months.

elements.element: The restriction permits Customer's internal development.
elements.evidence: Vacuously satisfied: no carve-out is needed because nothing prohibits development; § 12.4 as rendered expressly permits Customer to develop competing products, and § 12.3 confirms nothing restricts Customer from developing any product or service.

Vacuously satisfied: § 12.4 as rendered expressly permits Customer to "acquire any product or service that competes with Vendor," and § 12.3 preserves Customer's freedom to acquire; no acquisition prohibition remains.

elements.element: minimality: no duplication of existing operative language
elements.evidence: Retained § 12.3 already provides that "Nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service ... or conducting business in any field or territory." The new affirmative § 12.4 restates that same permission for competing products, adding a second operative freedom-of-action grant where simple deletion of the offending § 12.4 would have achieved the preferred position.

reasons: Preferred level is position-complete: the only preferred element — no non-compete or field-of-use restriction on Customer — is met in operative language, because the prohibitory second § 12.4 has been replaced by a permission and no residual term, territory, or post-term compete restraint binds Customer.

Fallback elements are vacuously met for the same reason (no restriction exists to be narrowed); the narrowed 12-month named-product alternative appears only in the margin comment and is therefore not operative — which is correct, since the preferred level is achieved.

Intent is preserved: the edit touches only the offending sentence, leaves § 12.3 intact and no longer contradicted, does not disturb the non-solicitation sentence in the first § 12.4, and creates no dangling cross-reference or undefined term.

Minimality fails on duplication. § 12.3 already states in operative terms that nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service in any field or territory; the rewritten § 12.4 re-grants that same freedom for competing products, duplicating an existing operative term. Repair: delete the prohibitory § 12.4 outright (strike the sentence) rather than substituting an affirmative permission, and rely on retained § 12.3 for Customer's freedom of action.

No other defect: the rationale correctly characterises the original as walk-away (24-month post-term restraint, undefined "any product or service ... in any territory") and correctly declines to double-flag the no-hire sentence under this rule.
